name: Nɔmaándɛ́
confidence_why: 5 independent first-hand sources agree (4 agree, 0 refine), none contradicts
catalog_citation: Wilkendorf, Patricia. 2001 [1998]. Sketch grammar of Nɔmaándɛ́: sections 1-4. Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon. 30 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives 47933; PDF via the Internet Archive capture of silcam.org)
catalog_locator: §2.2 'Suprasegmental Features', p. 6 = PDF p. 6 (page footer reads 6; the earlier locator 'printed p.7' is off by one). Syllable structure §2.4 on p. 7.
catalog_quote: Nɔmaandɛ is a tonal language with two phonemic tone levels, high and low. There is only one tone per vowel but a long vowel may have two different tones, resulting in high-low and low-high tone sequences. A high tone may be lowered in certain environments, such as verbal conjugations, which results in phonemic downstep. Phonetic downdrift also occurs on the sentence level with each high tone that occurs after a low tone being lower than the preceding high tone in the sentence.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: The source describes Nomaande prosody purely in terms of a two-level tone system (H, L; contours on long vowels; downstep; downdrift) and says nothing about word stress or accent; no stress rule can be extracted. Corroborated by Wilkendorf 1991 (p.62, two underlying tones, H/L/HL/LH stem melodies) and Boyd 2015 §2.2.5 ('Maande has a two-tone system underlyingly, high and low').
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Related prosodic facts noted: word-final vowels of nouns and verbs are devoiced except question-finally and in song (Wilkendorf 2001 §2.3; Boyd 2015 §2.2.2.3).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical/grammatical tone at word level and downdrift at sentence level; nothing on word- or phrase-level stress. Quote re-spaced by me: the PDF text layer is a +1-codepoint-shifted legacy font with spaces dropped; wording verified against the decoded layer.
new_statements.identity_note: All SIL descriptions (Scruggs, Taylor, Wilkendorf) and Boyd 2015 are based on the Nuceku dialect of Tchekos village (the reference dialect); Boyd calls the language 'Maande'. Same languoid as Glottolog noma1260 / ISO lem; no separate dialect glottocodes involved.

new_statements.quote: The basic tonal system in Nomaandé, a Bantu language of Central Cameroon classified as A.46 by Guthrie (1971:32) and as No. 512 by ALCAM (Dieu and Renaud 1983:53), consists of two underlying tones, high (H) and low (L). The canonical shape of Nomaandé noun stems is disyllabic of two major types—vcv and cvcv. Each noun stem, then, has an underlying tonal pattern of either H, L, HL, or LH. In addition, each stem has a noun class prefix that bears an underlying L.

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing statement from Wilkendorf 2001 (sketch grammar §2.2: two phonemic tone levels, no stress statement). Adds the noun-stem melody inventory and the locative tone rules but nothing on stress. The remaining chapters of the volume (Makaa, Kako, Nugunu, Podoko) are about other languages and were not scanned; a full-volume scanned at the box's current load (~350) ran at ~9 min/page and was abandoned after page 1 in favour of the preface and the Nɔmaándɛ́ pages.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nɔmaándɛ́ is described purely as a two-tone language (underlying H and L; noun-stem melodies H, L, HL, LH; noun-class prefixes underlyingly L; verb stems L or HL) with downdrift, downstep, floating H and tone-spreading rules. Neither the editor's preface nor the Nɔmaándɛ́ chapter mentions word stress, accent or prominence at all; the words 'stress'/'accent' occur nowhere in the scanned Preface or chapter (the only 'accent' hits are French 'mettre l'accent sur' = 'to focus on' in the preface).
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; tonal irregularities only (fn. 6 p. 64: two of five V-VCV nouns do not follow the locative tone rules)
new_statements.identity_note: Wilkendorf's chapter data come from Mr. Emmanuel Atoko of the village of Tchekos (fn. 1, p. 62); fn. 2 says the Lemande live in seven villages plus Bokito and that their dialects are mutually intelligible. Boyd 2015 also uses the Tchekos/Nuceku variety as reference dialect. No dialect-specific stress claim exists in any source.

new_statements.quote: The tonal complexity of Grassfields Bantu languages is well attested in the literature. Less-well attested, however, is the fact that many of the same kinds of tonal phenomena (downstep, downdrift, floating tones, tonal morphemes, toneless morphemes) are also quite frequent in Narrow Bantu languages, especially those of southern Cameroon. Since this volume contains descriptions of four of these languages, the extent to which Bantu languages of Zone A mirror the complexities of Grassfields Bantu languages can now be studied more closely.
